slides.title: Two complexity classes
slides.body:
**P** = problems solvable in polynomial time on a deterministic Turing machine. The 'tractable' class — algorithms exist that scale polynomially.

**NP** = problems whose solutions are *verifiable* in polynomial time. Or equivalently: solvable in polynomial time on a *nondeterministic* Turing machine.

**Note**: the 'NP' stands for 'Nondeterministic Polynomial,' NOT 'Non-Polynomial.' Common misconception ([[np-means-non-polynomial]]).

$P \subseteq NP$ (anything solvable in poly time is verifiable in poly time). The famous open question: does $NP \subseteq P$? I.e., is everything verifiable in poly time also *solvable* in poly time?

Most computer scientists believe $P \neq NP$. No proof either way. The Clay Institute offers $1M for either.

slides.title: NP-completeness
slides.body:
A problem is **NP-complete** if:
1. It's in NP.
2. Every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time ([[reductions]]).

NP-complete problems are the **hardest in NP** — if any has a polynomial algorithm, then all of NP is in P.

First NP-complete problem: **SAT** (Boolean satisfiability). Cook-Levin theorem (1971). Karp (1972) showed 21 other natural problems are also NP-complete via reductions from SAT.

Famous NP-complete problems:
- **3-SAT**: SAT restricted to 3-literal clauses.
- **Vertex cover**: smallest set of vertices touching every edge.
- **Hamiltonian cycle**: cycle visiting every vertex once.
- **Traveling salesman (decision)**: tour of cost $\leq k$?
- **Knapsack (decision)**: subset summing to $\geq v$ within weight $\leq W$?
- **3-coloring**: can graph be 3-colored?
- **Subset sum**: any subset sums to $T$?

If you find a polynomial algorithm for ANY of these, you've proven $P = NP$ and earned $1M.

question.question: Which of these correctly describes the relationship between P and NP?
options: P and NP are disjoint — they share no problems

P ⊆ NP (P is a subset of NP). Every problem in P is also in NP because if you can solve it in poly time, you can also verify a solution in poly time (just solve it). Whether NP ⊆ P is the famous open question
NP is always strictly larger than P
NP ⊂ P — every NP problem is in P
question.explanation: P is a subset of NP. Anything you can solve in polynomial time, you can also verify in polynomial time. The unknown direction is whether NP ⊆ P — i.e., whether everything that's verifiable is also solvable in poly time. Believed false but unproven; the canonical open problem in CS theory.

slides.title: Why we believe P ≠ NP
slides.body:
No proof. But:

1. **50+ years of intense effort** by the smartest minds in CS. No one has found a polynomial algorithm for any NP-complete problem.

2. **Many natural problems are NP-complete**. If any were in P, all NP-complete problems would be in P (via the reductions).

3. **All approaches hit barriers**. Algebraic methods, derandomization, pseudorandomness — every angle hits the 'natural proofs' barrier (Razborov-Rudich 1994).

The **practical implication**: for NP-complete problems, accept that exact solutions are intractable for large inputs. Use approximation algorithms ([[approximation-algorithms]]), randomized algorithms ([[randomized-algorithms]]), or specialized solvers (SAT solvers, ILP solvers).

Modern SAT solvers (CDCL-based: Glucose, MiniSAT, Lingeling) routinely solve million-variable instances. Worst-case is still exponential; practical SAT is far easier than the worst case because real instances have structure.

slides.title: How to handle NP-complete problems in practice
slides.body:
Don't waste time looking for a polynomial algorithm. Use:

1. **Approximation algorithms with provable bounds**. Vertex cover has 2-approximation. Set cover has $\ln n$-approximation. Metric TSP has 1.5-approximation (Christofides 1976).

2. **Heuristics**. No guarantees but often work. Genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, local search.

3. **ILP / MIP solvers**. Modern solvers (Gurobi, CPLEX, OR-Tools) handle real-world instances even when worst case is NP-hard.

4. **SAT solvers**. CDCL-based solvers handle million-variable instances despite NP-completeness.

5. **Special-case algorithms**. Many real-world instances of NP-complete problems have structure (sparsity, geometric structure, low treewidth) that admits polynomial algorithms.

6. **Fixed-parameter tractable (FPT)**: polynomial in $n$, exponential in some parameter $k$. Useful when $k$ is small.

7. **Randomized algorithms with probabilistic bounds**.

The boundary between 'NP-hard, intractable' and 'NP-hard, but practical solvers exist' is one of the most important practical insights in algorithm engineering.

slides.title: P, NP, and the gap nobody can close
slides.body:
**P**: decision problems solvable in polynomial time. ('Is this graph connected?' — yes/no in $O(V+E)$.)

**NP**: decision problems whose 'yes' answers are *verifiable* in polynomial time given a certificate. ('Is there a Hamiltonian cycle?' — given a cycle, you can verify it traverses every vertex once in $O(V)$.)

**P ⊆ NP** trivially (a polynomial solver is its own verifier). **Whether P = NP is the famous open question** — most computer scientists believe P ≠ NP but nobody has proved it.

**NP-complete**: the 'hardest' problems in NP. Every NP problem reduces to any NP-complete problem in polynomial time, so a polynomial algorithm for one NP-complete problem solves all of NP. Famous NP-completes: SAT, 3-COLORING, TSP-decision, KNAPSACK-decision, SUBSET-SUM, CLIQUE.

If you're stuck on a problem and someone says 'this is NP-complete', they're saying: don't expect a polynomial exact solution. Reach for approximation, heuristics, or constraint-restricted polynomial cases.

question.question: You're given that 3-SAT is NP-complete. You reduce your problem to 3-SAT in polynomial time. What does this prove?
options: Your problem is at most as hard as 3-SAT (it's in NP if your reduction is the right direction).
question.explanation: Reducing FROM your problem TO 3-SAT shows your problem is no harder than 3-SAT. To prove NP-completeness you need the OPPOSITE direction: reduce a known NP-complete problem TO your problem, showing your problem is at least as hard. Direction matters in reductions.

hints: Which direction of the reduction proves which inequality of hardness?
'My problem reduces to a known hard problem' vs 'a known hard problem reduces to mine'.
slides.workedSolution: A polynomial reduction from $A$ to $B$ shows $A$ is no harder than $B$. So reducing YOUR problem to 3-SAT shows your problem is no harder than 3-SAT (i.e., it's in NP if 3-SAT is). To prove NP-completeness you'd reduce 3-SAT (or any known NP-complete problem) TO your problem — showing yours is at least as hard.

question.question: NP-complete in disguise
question.prompt: You're asked to assign one of three colors to each room in a floor plan such that no two adjacent rooms share a color. A teammate says 'how hard could that be — let's just try all colorings'. Why might that explode, and what's the textbook label for this problem?
Explain in two sentences why P vs NP isn't just a theoretical question.
